evidence/reviews/faa-wildlife-strike-sub.reason: A row is one consolidated FAA strike record (field list: INDEX NR is an 'Individual record number'; SOURCE can be 'Multiple' report types). The entities that recur across rows - airframe (REG), airport (AIRPORT_ID) and operator (OPID) - are not usable: REG is dropped, AIRPORT_ID is never resolved by build.py, and OPID is collapsed to a five-value class, so no entity key exists in the release. The dependence the release can express is shared exposure on a calendar day: possible repeat records of one encounter, several aircraft meeting the same flock, and common weather or migration conditions. incident_date is the contract's declared event key and time column (construction.json:137, 586), is a real source field rather than a constructed key, is not a declared predictor (build.py:17-21), is never missing (build.py:441-443 drops unparseable dates) and is written to the holdout by the same code as the public splits (build.py:22, 674). It contains every state-by-day grouping and gives roughly 1,461 clusters of about 17 rows in the 2019-2022 holdout. Public training metadata supports it modestly: pairs of positives on the same day exceed a within-year-month label shuffle in train (589 observed vs 523.4 +/- 23.1, z 2.84) and in the same direction in eval (65 vs 55.8 +/- 7.2, z 1.27); narrowing to state plus day shows no additional excess (train 42 vs 31.8 +/- 5.0; eval 3 vs 3.1 +/- 1.9), and state alone shows none once month is controlled (train z -0.26, eval z -0.78). Row-level independence was rejected because unique record numbers do not show independence when recurring airframes, airports and operators are unobserved. Chosen from source meaning and public train/eval metadata before any holdout scoring; no holdout rows or holdout metrics were read.
limitations: Airframe, airport and operator identity are not carried, so dependence from the same aircraft, airport or operator recurring on different days cannot be clustered. state is the only persistent geographic column; it showed no detectable label clustering in public data, which is weak evidence about airport-level dependence.

The measured day-level dependence is modest: the excess is about 12 percent more same-day positive pairs in train, is within noise in eval (z 1.27), and disappears against a within-year shuffle (train z 0.07, eval z 0.42). The key is a conservative guard, not strongly measured dependence.

Day clusters assume independence across days. They do not absorb seasonal or multi-year drift; the positive rate falls from about 5.8 percent in 1990 to 0.4 percent in 2018 and is 0.42 percent in the holdout per meta.json. Intervals from day-cluster resampling describe sampling variability within 2019-2022, not transport to other periods.

incident_date is the strike date, not the report date or the database-entry date. Dependence created by entry or adjudication batches is not captured; index_nr ranges are associated with the label within every public year, which suggests such batches exist.
Positives are rare: meta.json implies 107 in the holdout, about one per 14 days, so most day clusters contain no positive and cluster-resampled AUC and calibration estimates will be unstable.
A day cluster pools strikes from all states. This is coarser than state-by-day and therefore conservative for same-location dependence, but it treats unrelated same-day strikes as one unit.
The holdout was not inspected, so the cluster count, sizes and the persistence of the same-day pattern there are inferred from the contract and public splits, not observed.

evidence.rule: Retain rows with incident_date from 1990-01-01 through 2022-12-31, state in the 50 U.S. states or DC, at least one of ac_class or ac_mass present after normalising missing tokens, and damage in N, M, M?, S or D. Blank damage is dropped and never labelled 0. Nonblank unexpected damage codes in that base population fail construction.
